canonicalExplanation.summary: Every real HTML page shares the same skeleton: `<!doctype html>` switches the browser into **standards mode**, `<html lang="en">` says the page's language, `<head>` holds information *about* the page (encoding, title, viewport), and `<body>` holds what people see. Put `<meta charset="utf-8">` **first** in the head so every character is read correctly.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
You open your page and "café" shows up with two stray symbols where the é should be, and the layout is subtly off compared to your friend's copy. Both problems come from a missing skeleton. A page begins with <!doctype html>, sets lang on html, gives a title in head, and puts visible content in body. In this lesson you'll create and explain a complete minimal HTML document with an early encoding declaration.

sections.heading: Head vs body

includes: Write a complete minimal document with doctype, lang, charset, viewport and title.
Explain what belongs in head versus body.

outcomes: Create and explain a complete minimal HTML document with early encoding declaration.

examples.title: The smallest complete page
examples.situation: A page begins with <!doctype html>, sets lang on html, gives a title in head, and puts visible content in body.
walkthrough: **Begins with <!doctype html>:** the browser renders in standards mode.
**Sets lang on html and a title in head:** `<html lang="en">`, then `<meta charset="utf-8">` first and `<title>Asha's Recipes</title>`.
**Visible content in body:** the h1 and paragraph go inside `<body>`.
examples.result: The tab reads "Asha's Recipes", accented text displays correctly, and the page renders in standards mode.

examples.title: The garbled café
examples.situation: A page saved as UTF-8 has no charset declaration. "café" shows with two stray symbols in place of the é on some computers.
walkthrough: Without a declaration, the browser guesses an older encoding.
The two UTF-8 bytes of é are read as two separate characters.
Fix: add `<meta charset="utf-8">` as the first element in head.
examples.result: With the early declaration, café displays correctly everywhere.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The doctype is an optional comment that only documents the HTML version.
misconceptions.correction: The doctype is required: it tells browsers to use standards mode. Without it, pages render in quirks mode, where layout rules differ.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what mode does a page without a doctype use?

analogy.example: The skeleton is like a **letter**: the envelope format (doctype), the language it's written in (lang), the address label (title, charset in head), and the letter itself (body).
usefulFor: remembering head = about the page, body = the page
limitations: Letters don't switch rendering modes; browsers do.
A letter has one reader; pages serve screen readers, search engines and browsers.

steps.explanation: The page begins with the doctype, so the browser uses standards mode.
It sets lang on html and gives a title in head after the early charset.
It puts visible content in body.

remediation.explanation: Keep a checklist at the top of every file: **doctype → html lang → head (charset first, viewport, title) → body**. Tick each before writing content.

recap.summary: To create a complete minimal HTML document, start with <!doctype html>, set lang on html, put meta charset utf-8 first in head with a viewport and title, and place visible content in body. The doctype switches on standards mode.
